claim: The data covers 1,656 conversations, described by 3,312 person-level rows from 1,456 distinct participants.
Every one of the 1,656 conversations appears exactly twice in the person-level table, once for each partner, and the conversation-level table has one row per conversation.
The rating scales differ by item: affect and enjoyment run 1 to 9, liking, meta-perceived liking, shared reality and politics run 1 to 7 or 1 to 6, and loneliness runs 1 to 3.
Of the participants who reported their sex, 53.4% are female, 44.9% male and 1.6% other or prefer not to answer.
Participants average 34.3 years old, with a median of 32 and a range from 19 to 66; the middle half falls between 25 and 41.
The sample is majority white (64.8%), then Asian (14.9%), Black or African American (7.6%), Hispanic or Latino (6.8%) and mixed (3.9%).
40.4% of participants hold a bachelor's degree, 24.0% have some college, 18.7% a master's degree and only 6.5% finished high school or less.
The politics variable only ever takes the values 1, 2, 3, 4 and 6 - never 5 - with 36.7% of participants at 4 and 27.8% at 6.
Average mood climbs through the conversation: 6.10 before it starts, 6.16 at the beginning, 6.93 in the middle, 7.38 at the end, with the rating for the conversation overall at 7.32.
Arousal rises alongside mood, from 5.32 before the call to 5.67 at its beginning, 6.40 in the middle and 6.70 at the end.
Individually, mood rises by 1.23 points on average from the beginning to the end of the conversation (median 1.0) across 3,257 participants.
Of the 3,257 participants with both ratings, 2,153 (66%) felt better at the end of the conversation than at the beginning, 856 felt exactly the same and 248 (8%) felt worse.
The lower people's mood at the start, the more it improved: those starting at 1 gained 4.00 points on average, those starting at 5 gained 1.93, and those starting at 9 lost 0.21.
Even in conversations people enjoyed, mood swung: the worst moment of the conversation averaged 5.80 and the best moment 7.83, against an end-of-conversation average of 7.38.
Enjoyment is rated high and skewed positive: 23.7% of reports are 7, 25.7% are 8 and 28.6% are the maximum 9, so 78.0% of the 3,257 ratings are 7 or above and only 4.7% are 4 or below.
On the 1-to-7 liking scale, participants rate how much they like their partner at 6.00 but rate how much their partner likes them at only 5.35, a gap of 0.64 points.
1,691 participants like their partner more than they think their partner likes them, 1,412 put the two at the same value, and only 154 think they are liked less than they like.
The gap is not an artefact of scale use: matching each person to their partner's actual answer, partners really did report liking them by 6.00 on average while they guessed only 5.35.
Guesses about a partner's liking are barely informative: they correlate only r = 0.19 with how much that partner actually said they liked them.
Liking is also only weakly mutual: how much one person likes their partner correlates r = 0.19 with how much that partner likes them back.
The same discount runs through trait judgements: partners rate each other's intelligence at 7.68 on average but think the other rates them at only 7.06, and kindness at 7.98 against a guessed 7.43.

The two people in a conversation disagree about how it went: their enjoyment ratings correlate only r = 0.18, differ by 1.43 points on average on the 9-point scale, and match exactly in just 25.7% of pairs.
code: people.assign(w=people.groupby('convo_id').cumcount()).pivot(index='convo_id', columns='w', values='how_enjoyable').pipe(lambda d: pd.Series({'within_pair_r': d.corr().iloc[0,1], 'mean_abs_diff': (d[0]-d[1]).abs().mean(), 'exact_agreement': (d[0]==d[1]).mean(), 'pairs': d.dropna().shape[0]}))

claim: At conversation level, how much the pair likes each other is the closest correlate of enjoyment (r = 0.87), then the 0-to-100 conversationalist score (0.78), thinking your partner likes you (0.75), rating your partner kind (0.62), having things in common (0.59) and shared reality (0.57).
The conversationalist score is a 0-to-100 slider averaging 73.9 across the 1,603 conversations that have it, with a median of 76.5 and a middle half from 65.5 to 85.
Matching partners on sex changes enjoyment hardly at all: same-sex pairs average 7.44 across 1,534 ratings and mixed-sex pairs 7.38 across 1,723.
Race matching goes the other way but by just as little: pairs of different races average 7.46 enjoyment over 1,815 ratings versus 7.34 for same-race pairs over 1,442.

Political distance only slowly erodes enjoyment: pairs with identical politics average 7.48 (408 conversations), pairs 2 points apart 7.41 (494), pairs 4 points apart 7.15 (115) and pairs 5 points apart 7.07 (23).
Age distance costs common ground but not pleasure: how much pairs have in common falls from 6.18 at age_diff 0 to 5.27 at age_diff 40, while enjoyment goes the other way, from 7.43 to 7.63.

What matters is not similarity but agreement about the conversation itself: when the two partners' shared-reality ratings are close (shared_reality_diff 0 or 1) enjoyment averages 7.52 and 7.54, but it falls to 6.96 at a gap of 3 and 6.44 at a gap of 4.

Status is systematically under-claimed: people rate their own status at 5.53, guess their partner rates it at 5.74, while partners actually rate it at 5.91, and they rate their partner's status highest of all at 5.91.
On the turn-length rating, people give their own turns 5.40 on average and their partner's 5.03, and the two are negatively related across conversations (r = -0.42), as if talk time were a fixed pie.
People rate themselves lonelier than they rate their partner, 1.80 against 1.55 on a 1-to-3 scale, though the two are answered by different numbers of people (1,172 and 2,952).
Perceiving your partner as lonely goes with a worse conversation: your_loneliness correlates -0.22 with enjoyment, while your own loneliness correlates only -0.06.
Among individual ratings, shared reality correlates 0.53 with how much you like your partner, 0.58 with enjoyment and 0.52 with thinking your partner likes you.
